subtopic: SUGGESTED DIVISION INTO TWO SECTIONS- AGRICULTURAL AND WHEAT
SUGGESTED DIVISION INTO TWO SECTIONS- AGRICULTURAL AND WHEAT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the agricultural committee would give much better satisfaction if it were divided into two sections: (a) agricultural section; (b) wheat section.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, in offering a few
words in support of this resolution, I intend no discourtesy towards the grain growers. I move this resolution simply with the object of getting a committee that will function better, at least as regards eastern agriculture. At the present time and for some years past it has been impossible in the committee on agriculture to discuss agricultural problems relating to eastern Canada, and I should like to have that committee divided in such a manner that these questions may be discussed in a sane way. At the present time and for many years past the committee on agriculture has consisted of an overwhelming number of grain growers who have just swamped the eastern section of that committee and it has been impossible, as I say, to discuss properly matters connected with eastern agriculture. The committee is composed of sixty members, twenty-seven of whom are grain growers, nine or ten genuine farmers from the east and the twenty-four or twenty-three who make up the remaining number, representing medicine, law, dentistry and almost every other calling that we have in this country. Under such circumstances it is hard to imagine how eastern agriculture can be discussed with any clearness in that committee.
I want to pay my respects to the grain, grower; I admit he is a number one good fellow and good citizen, but he is just as loquacious and aggressive as you can find. Tie never misses an opportunity of telling you all about any subject you may want to [DOT]bring up; he imagines he knows it all. This i[Mr. Ralston.)
is a superiority complex which has been developed in the past, when between the year 1921 and 1930 the wheat growers were directing the destiny of this country.
I should like to call to the attention of the house some of the grievances facing eastern farmers. Especially since 1925 the east has been in a bad condition. The late government apparently did everything in its power to put it out of business. Further, I am forced to admit that the present administration is not exerting itself to the extent I had wished. It is with some reluctance I take upon myself the task of bringing this to the attention of the house. The importance and urgency of the matter demands that something be done at once, if we are to save eastern agriculture. This should not be made a matter of political controversy. Both of the major parties in this house for a great many years have been negligent of the interests of the eastern farmers. There are a few genuine farmers in this house, some of whom have been here for many years. Even they do not seem to be willing to accept the task of speaking for eastern agriculture. Perhaps their unwillingness may be the result of their longer and greater political experience. However that may be, Mr. Speaker, I am going to do my best to fulfil my promise to help my farmer friends. I trust that the house will charitably accept my observations in the spirit in which they are given. It is my intention to make some constructive suggestions with the sole object of aiding the government in some small measure, so that it may come to the rescue of the biggest and best class of citizens in our dominion.
In 1925, 1926 and 1930 I was told from every platform in my counties that it would be impossible to do anything in this house to help the farmers. I do not believe that such is the case. The great trouble in this chamber has been that hon. members did not know how to help eastern farmers. I purpose to tell of the grievances under which those farmers are labouring, and I am presumptuous enough to believe that I can suggest ways and means of relieving their difficulties.

subtopic: SUGGESTED DIVISION INTO TWO SECTIONS- AGRICULTURAL AND WHEAT
speechtext: How about changing the government?

subtopic: SUGGESTED DIVISION INTO TWO SECTIONS- AGRICULTURAL AND WHEAT
speechtext:
I have been engaged in mixed farming all my life. Without boasting idly, I flatter myself that I know the game from A to Z. I want to add that it has been an expensive experience, and anybody who has been engaged in agriculture the last few years will not doubt my words. I have the honour to represent a double constituency,

Agriculture Committee-Mr. Picket
composed of those two fine counties Brome and Missisquoi, situated in the eastern section of the province of Quebec. I was elected by my farmer friends on the distinct promise that I would do what I could to help them, and to the best of my ability I shall attempt to fill my promise. I can but say, in the words of Lincoln, "I am not bound to win, but I am bound to be true; I am not bound to succeed, but I am bound to live up to what light I have." Knowing that there are several ways in which the farming industry could be beneficially assisted, I should be remiss in my duty were I not to bring my suggestions to the attention of the House of Commons, the body which has the power, if it will exercise that power, greatly to help the farmer out of the abyss in which he finds himself. I have been a member in this house for about two and a half year's, and during the two long and one short sessions I have been a regular attendant. Now I find I have made a good beginning on a third session.
I submit we have had very few practical suggestions, let alone any material legislation, for the benefit of dairymen. That fact in itself seems rather strange. I have listened anxiously and patiently for some of the farmers in this house to say a word for eastern agriculture, but up to the present time we have not heard one practical constructive suggestion from either side of the house. The opposition never misses an opportunity of portraying the calamitous conditions under which eastern farmers are working, and have no hesitation in denouncing the present government therefor, despite the fact that hon. members opposite, when they occupied this side of the house, gave the farmers their death blow through the Australian trade treaty of 1925. The New Zealand order in council which remained in force until October 25, 1930, proved most destructive to the interests of the farmers. They have not been able to regain their former prestige and will not do so for some time. In 1922 the then government, the present opposition, enacted the Hog Grading Act, and in 1925 the Egg Grading Act. The unfair, irrational and unjust administration of both of these acts has proved a curse to the farmers. In the past two or three sessions it has been the regular pastime of some hon. members opposite to compare prices. They state that butter is so much in Canada and so much in the United States, eggs so much in Canada and so much in the United States. Particularly, that was the pleasant pastime in which the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard) indulged. To-day however we do not hear so much cackling. I would like to remind the house
that all kinds of farm produce, with the exception of beef, are selling for higher prices in Canada to-day than anywhere else in the world.

subtopic: SUGGESTED DIVISION INTO TWO SECTIONS- AGRICULTURAL AND WHEAT
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: SUGGESTED DIVISION INTO TWO SECTIONS- AGRICULTURAL AND WHEAT
speechtext:
That is absolutely true.
Hon. members do not realize it because they do not hear that side of the question discussed. While farmers in the United States are receiving only ten or twelve cents a dozen for eggs, in Canada they are receiving twenty cents or more. While butter costs only sixteen or seventeen cents in the United States it costs twenty cents in Canada. We do not hear so many comparisons of prices as we did.

subtopic: SUGGESTED DIVISION INTO TWO SECTIONS- AGRICULTURAL AND WHEAT
speechtext: What is the price in New Zealand?

subtopic: SUGGESTED DIVISION INTO TWO SECTIONS- AGRICULTURAL AND WHEAT
speechtext:
A good deal less than it is here. During my short sojourn in this house I have learned a few things, from observation and experience; not the least of these is that this house is not in sympathy with eastern agriculture. That seems strange. The eastern farmers constitute by far the largest class in this country. We all realize that the government is endeavouring to do everything it can to get us out of the terrible condition we are in, and to my mind, helping eastern farmers to increase their purchasing power would go a long way in that direction. I propose to tell you how this can be brought about without increasing the cost to the consumer.
To repeat, I say that this house is not of a dairying mentality. When agriculture is mentioned in this house the great majority of the members at once commence to think of grain growing. In grain growing we have a short seasonal occupation, seed time and harvest, with three or four months intervening which the growers devote principally to local and domestic visiting and social amenities of one kind or another and studying ail sorts of abstract political theories such as inflation and deflation, currency revaluation, increase of the price level, parity of the pound and dollar, and so on. To my mind, inflation is equivalent to destruction, damnation and dissolution of the country. After harvest these same gentlemen -barring the last two years-fortified by a large bank roll, take occasion to tour the world. They make large amounts of money, but Canada does not get any benefit from it; it is spent in foreign countries. The western grain grower cannot stand the rigors of a Canadian winter; he has to go to southern beaches where the gentle zephyrs blow through his whiskers, cooling his heated brow. I do not blame him one bit; I
1920	.	COMMONS
Agriculture Committee-Mr. Pickel
would do the same thing if 1 could. And I do not know that I can blame him for trying to put these things over on the east. But it is high time that the grain growers should recognize that there is an east, and to appreciate the fact that it is all due to the east that there is a west at all. They should also appreciate that where there is one farmer west of lake Superior there are three east. The westerner is a sort of migratory farmer; he goes away with the birds in the fall and comes back with them in the spring.

subtopic: SUGGESTED DIVISION INTO TWO SECTIONS- AGRICULTURAL AND WHEAT
speechtext: He doesn't take the eggs with him.

subtopic: SUGGESTED DIVISION INTO TWO SECTIONS- AGRICULTURAL AND WHEAT
speechtext:
Referring back to the agriculture committee. I want to say that whenever an easterner gets up in that committee and begins to talk milk, eggs, butter, anything of the kind, the western grain growers will take the words right out of his mouth. Seventy-five per cent of them use canned milk, and they do not want to be tied down to a cow, for if they are they cannot go south. Theirs is the glorious carefree life! Contrast this orgy of existence with the hard, plodding life of the eastern farmer. He puts in the longest hours of continuous and exacting labour for the least remuneration of any oloss in the world. His is not a short seasonal occupation; it is continuous from day to day and from year to year all his life. He has to be on the job over six hundred eight hour days a year without respite or holiday. That is the life of the eastern farmer.
The eastern farmer is endowed with a peculiar mentality; the great difficulty he has is that he is non-cooperative. The western-farmers, on the other hand, all hang together. I would counsel the farmers of eastern Canada to send more representatives from the rural sections, members whose interests are their interests. I think the welfare of the farmer's would be better looked after if there were more rural representation. If the eastern agriculturist were better represented in this house it would be much better for the house' and for the country. I firmly believe that if there had been a good strong representation here of eastern farmers we would not have built the Grand Trunk Pacific, nor yet the Hudson Bay railway. The eastern farmer is faced with a continuous struggle for existence; he has the heavenly elements to fighb- drought, flood, wind, frost, hail; he has numberless enemies in nature, many varieties of parasites, flies, worms, grubs and bugs. Everything he raises is the result of continuous and hard labour. One would naturally think that when he had brought his crop or product to maturity his labours would be about finished,

but, sir, such is not the case. When he comes to put his product on the market and tries to secure a little return for his labour he meets another set of pests, even worse than the others. I refer to middlemen, commission men, inspection acts, irrational and unfair administration of grading acts, governmental interference, regulations and restrictions, and by no means least, the politician. That is what the eastern farmer is up against.
Now the politician means well, but in the majority of cases he has not the slightest idea of what could and should be done to help the farmer; so adverse instead of beneficial legislation is often enacted than otherwise. For instance, we hear advocated the formation of an export marketing board. That seems to be a sort of shibboleth in this house. To my mind, sir, we do not need an export marketing hoard at all. We certainly do not need it for the east; if it can do anything for the west I am for it and will do anything I can to further it.
Here I would like to put on Hansard the percentage of Canadian agricultural production consumed in the domestic market. Excluding wheat and cheese, nearly 97 per cent of all farm produce is consumed here in Canada; excluding wheat, 95-7 per cent; including wheat, 88 per cent. The eastern farmer lias nothing of any consequence to export, just a little cheese. Of oats, 100 per cent is consumed in Canada; of barley, 100 per cent; of rye, 100 per cent; of flax seed, 100 per cent; of milk, condensed, and milk products, 100 per cent; of eggs, 100 per cent. Red clover is the article of which we consume least, namely 27-7 per cent.

I have figures, 1931-32. Right at home, under our very noses the eastern farmer is being exploited and profiteered against by the middleman and the commission man. These people apparently have no difficulty in securing the necessary legislation from the different governing bodies to enable them to take advantage of the farmer, and that is the trouble with the eastern farmer to-day.
In support of my contention I bring to your notice the condition of the milk trade. In my section of the country, fifty-five miles from Montreal, 75 per cent of all the milk produced is consumed fresh as fluid milk or cream; 57 per cent and a decimal of all the milk produced in the entire dominion is consumed as fresh milk or cream, 25 per cent is made into butter, 6 per cent into cheese, and 7 per cent and a decimal into milk products-evaporated milk and milk products. The great bulk of the produce of the farmers in the east is milk; that is what the farmer depends upon principally for his income.
In the city of Montreal during the past season the farmers in my section have received a net of 70 cents a hundred pounds for milk. They are supposed to get $1.35, and they must pay 25 cents express to the city as well as cartage from the station, and then they are penalized because they are told that they are sending too much. The distributor tells them that they have so much milk that they have to separate it, and therefore the farmer has to take butter prices. This brings his net down to 70 cents and even as low as 60; at any rate it varies between 60 and 80.
The Montreal market, even at that low price, is the best market w'e have, and the result is that more milk and cream is sent to the city than is consumed as fresh milk or cream. Consequently much of this milk is churned, so that the farmers have to be content with a butter price. That is the farmer's side of the story. On the other hand, the distributor, when he sells that milk, receives $4 per hundred, if he distributes in quarts, at 10 cents a quart, and he gets 2 cents a quaiit extra if he distributes by the pint. If you consider the spread he gets out
of ice cream, which costs him 37i cents a gallon and which he sells at $1.20, and consider the buttermilk which he steals entirely from the farmer and sells for nearly as much as he does whole milk, and if you consider further the separated milk which he uses to reduce the super-standard milk which he also steals from the farmer, you will readily see that he is getting more than $5 per hundred. How in the world such an unjust condition of affairs can be permitted to exist in this supposedly civilized country is more than I can imagine. It is absolute robbery.
Now the farmer does not wish to boost the price to the consumer, who is paying enough already; 95 per cent of the consumers in the city, if you asked them, would tell you that the farmers are robbing them. That is simply propaganda spread by the milkman to cover up his wickedness. He tries to pull the wool over people's eyes and make them think he is engaged in some philanthropic undertaking instead of staging a genuine holdup.
The farmer should have a fifty-fifty break in regard to the selling price in the city; he is entitled to it and should have it. The farmer in eastern Canada is not asking for a dole or a bonus or anything of that sort. Come to Quebec if you want to see thrifty, industrious people. Come and see our farmers. Let me say that the agitators in the southeast corner of the chamber will not have much weight in Quebec; they will not get any sympathy and so they will not come there. The older I get the firmer I am in my conviction that the greatest asset the dominion has is the French Canadian race. These people are the bulwarks of Canadianism; there is no question about it. Come there and go amongst them and you will see that they are busy people. They do not travel, but stay at home and attend to their business.
Right here I want to tell the western grain growers that there is a great potential market in the east for them if they will only take advantage of it. We should not be making butter in the east. We make the poorest butter in the world. It is humiliating to tell the farmer of eastern Canada that his butter is no good, but it is a fact. Whenever we send a consignment of butter to England, which is rare, it is at the bottom as regards grade and price; it receives the lowest price in the world. But when we send a box of cheese it is of superior quality. Our cheese is on top; it is the best cheese in the world.
It is a sad reflection on the Canadian people that we have been making butter for years and years when we could have done so much better making cheese. Last summer we made butter 'that sold at 15, 16 and 17 cents, where-
1922	COMMONS
Agriculture Committee-Mr. Tummon
as if we had made cheese we could have got as much as 22 to 25 cents. Let our people in the west make butter and everyone else in Canada make .cheese; let us specialize in it. We make an article that the English market requires.
Let us note the trend of the trade. In 1904 we exported 247,000,000 pounds of cheese to England; last year we exported 74,000,000 pounds. In 1904 New Zealand sent hardly any cheese to that market; last year they exported 250,000,000 pounds. They have usurped our place in the English market so far as volume is concerned; nevertheless we maintain the supremacy of our quality and price. Our cheese is the best; let us specialize in it. The government is possessed of all these facts and should organize an educational campaign throughout the east to assist the people in every way possible in the making of cheese.
Returning now to the milk situation, in the cities the different inspectors, the officials of the board of health and the legislatures seem to vie with one another in passing restrictive legislation at the request of the distributors for the purpose of keeping the small man out. The distributor builds great big palaces of plate glass and marble, moving into new premises every few years, and the farmer pays the price. Go into the streets of Montreal and stop before some apartment house in which there are fifteen or twenty families and you will see half a dozen milk trucks. They are just as extravagant in their operations as they can be. They do not curtail; the farmer is an easy mark and he pays the price. There are times when one may be pardoned for experiencing a sort of sentimental charitableness towards a pickpocket or a robber who takes long chances to gain his end, but there is no charity that anyone can feel towards the milk distributor who is daily guillotining and robbing the farmer, taking no chances at all himself. The milk distributor is gouging and robbing the farmer, he takes no chance at all as he is protected by legislation. I do not blame the Dominion government for the irregularities connected with the distribution of milk but I consider this house supreme, we have the power and it is within our jurisdiction to investigate the whole situation. The public should know at once who is responsible, there should be no hesitation in investigating this matter fully.

Mr. Speaker, in making a few remarks as seconder of this resolution I do not propose to draw any comparisons between the farmers in one part of Canada with those in any other part, nor do I intend to take up the time of the house in referring to many of the subjects already covered by the mover of the resolution (Mr. Pickel). The resolution reads:
That in the opinion of this house, the agricultural committee would give much better satisfaction if it were divided into tivo sections: (a) agricultural section; (b) wheat section.
I think the hon. member for Brome is to be congratulated for bringing this matter to the attention of the house. The subject matter of this resolution has been discussed privately by many members of the committee. I believe the usefulness of this committee could be increased by the adoption of the resolution. Like the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, I do not want the house to think for one moment that I feel that the questions which have been discussed in the past by the agriculture committee were not necessary or were not justly and properly discussed. I believe that these questions were important and were properly brought before the committee, but the fact remains that there have been certain years when practically the entire time of the committee has been taken up with questions of the grading and marketing of wheat, of barley and such like. There has been a feeling which has been not only confined to the members of the committee, that problems affecting the farmers in eastern and central Canada have been crowded out. This may be very largely due to the fact that the farmers of western Canada are more ready than those of eastern and central Canada to bring their problems to the attention of the government. As we all know, there is a proper way to get these different problems before that committee.
I went back a number of years to find out just how many meetings had been held annually by this committee and the subjects that had been discussed each year. I found that in 1922 there were twenty-seven meetings, twenty-two being in connection with wheat marketing and five in connection with questions relating to other forms of agriculture. In 1923 there were seventeen meetings held, none of which related to wheat or grain. That would seem to show that when questions concerning the marketing of wheat or the Canada Grain Act were not before the committee, the committee found time to deal

Agriculture Committee-Mr. Seguin
with questions relating to other parts of Canada. In 1924 there were seven meetings, two in connection with wheat rust and five in connection with other matters. In 1925 there were thirty-two meetings, twenty-six being in connection with wheat and the grain act and only six in connection with problems affecting other parts of Canada. In 1926 there were seven meetings held in connection with the grain act and two in connection with other problems. In 1927 seven meetings were held, all in connection with problems other than wheat and grain. In 1928 there were twenty-seven meetings, twenty-four in connection with the Canada Grain Act and the protein content of grain, and three in connection with other farm products. In 1929 forty meetings were held in connection with the protein content and grading generally of wheat. In 1930 fifty-one meetings were held, forty-nine of which were in connection with the grain act revision and two in connection with the maple sugar industry, a matter of much importance to the province from which the mover of this resolution comes. In 1931 there were seventeen meetings in connection with farm problems generally, and five in connection with the Whiteside inquiry. In 1932 there were ten meetings in connection with grain and six in connection with the beet sugar industry. In ten years there were one hundred and eighty-five meetings in connection with wheat, the grading of wheat and the like, and only seventy-one in connection with other problems affecting the farming industry of Canada.
As I said before, I am not questioning the importance of the questions relating to wheat; rather I feel that the committee at all times should be prepared to give whatever time is necessary to matters which relate to the marketing of grain and such like in the west. However, I do not think that the time of the committee should be taken up wholly in the discussion of such matters; some provision should be made whereby other branches of agriculture could be discussed. The growing of wheat is important to a great portion of the west, but there are other agricultural products which are just- as important to other sections of Canada. For instance in the dairy industry the district, from which I come, is particularly interested. The growing of potatoes is important to the maritime provinces; the growing of fruit is important to parts of Nova Scotia, Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia, and there is also the live stock problem, the poultry problem, and other matters which are important to many sections
of the country. I am convinced that some effort should be made to increase the usefulness of the agriculture committee, and I trust that the government and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) will look sympathetically upon this resolution.

I do know, however, that at the present time there is no place in which eastern agricultural problems are discussed; at least we can admit that. For instance there is a question which is vital to the milk producers of the eastern townships, that is butter. We were told a few minutes ago that our entire production of butter is consumed in Canada. We know furthermore that our Canadian production is idequate to the requirements of Canada. But the market and the price of butter appear to have been bedevilled by the possibility of importation from New Zealand. The disparity between the value of New Zealand money and our own and English money and our own has done much to nullify the benefit of the protective measures enacted by this government some months ago, so far as the butter producer is concerned. From time to time a few pounds of New Zealand butter come into the country, no large quantity came during the last year and a half, but
there is the constant menace, with the result that butter is being sold at extremely low prices, which is very discouraging to that large element in southeastern Quebec that is engaged almost exclusively in that industry. If a certain part of the time of the sessions of the agriculture committee were allotted to the discussion of questions of this kind, or if a subdivision of the committee were to devote time to problems of this type, that element which now feels itself almost without representation and without opportunity of making known its situation would feel that something had been done to alleviate its distress. If, as stated by the hon. gentleman who spoke last, there are large interests in the west producing butter, eggs, cheese, poultry and possibly tobacco, it seems to me that they should welcome this opportunity of studying these problems. I do not think it would necessarily follow, if a subcommittee were set up or a certain portion of the time of the present committee were devoted to these problems, that east would be set against west. If these interests exist in the west as they do in the east, then both have a common interest in going into these matters and seeing whether the condition of those engaged in this type of production cannot be improved.

He made also reference to legislation enacted within the last four or five years with regard to grading, he mentioned particularly hog-grading and egg-grading. Personally I am not possessed of information to qualify me to express an opinion as to the value of this legislation, but I do know that large elements feel that this legislation is burdensome. If it is beneficial, and if results are being achieved which warrant the expense of applying it, it would be a valuable service if the facts could be made known, because at the present time great numbers of the farming community feel that this legislation serves mainly one purpose, that of providing positions of emolument for the incumbents.

1928	COMMONS
Agriculture Committee-Mr. Vallance
He says:
That, in the opinion of this house, the agriculture committee would give much better satisfaction if it were divided into two sections: (a) agriculture section; (b) wheat section.
As I say, if the adoption of this resolution would remedy the ills he mentioned, I am all for it, but otherwise I am absolutely against it. I have been privileged since 1925 to be a member of the agriculture committee. The statistics that have been presented to-day by the hon. member for South Hastings (Mr. Tummon) do not present a true picture. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi charged that the western members are more aggressive; I admit it, but probably that is the reason we have at least attempted to grapple with the problems of western agriculture. I hasten to assure him that the same problems which he says are facing eastern agriculture to-day are facing western agriculture. During the years 1 have been privileged to sit on that committee I can assure the house that if they will consult the various reports that have been tabled they will find that we have discussed everything pertaining to agriculture; chickens, potatoes, butter, pork and pork products, the marketing and improvement of cattle, horses, etc. I have never known a question referred to the agriculture committee during the years I have sat on it that did not originate in this house or was not sent by some responsible minister of the crown, either the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Immigration and Colonization or the Minister of Trade and Commerce. If, as the hon. member contends, the eastern agriculturists have not had a fair break on the agriculture committee it is their own fault, they have the right to bring up on the floor of this house resolutions asking that certain matters be dealt with, and never in my experience has the committee refused to discuss them. One reason stands out preeminently in my mind for opposing the division of this committee, it is this; we have 245 members of this house, the greater number of them from the seats east of the great lakes, and if the problems of western agriculture are going to be discussed intelligently, without monopolizing the time of the house, the place is the floor of that committee, and representatives of various provinces east of the great lakes should find themselves in that committee, if not to contribute to the debates, at least to get some knowledge of the position. I think those members from eastern Canada who have been on the agriculture committee will admit that sitting in and listening to the discussion has been an education to them.

In connection with the figures given by the hon. member for South Hastings, we did revise the Canada Grain Act along about 1928, and I think he charged the committee with setting up a special committee or subcommittee that dealt entirely with the wheat problem and consolidation of the Canada Grain Act. There is no reason, even as the committee is constituted to-day, to prevent a subcommittee from discussing any problem pertaining to agriculture in any of its aspects. One would judge from the remarks of the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi that all we do in western Canada is grow wheat or cereals. During the two months we sat here last fall I had the privilege of attending the Royal Winter Fair, and it amazed me the way western Canada scooped most of the prizes for cattle there. Does that indicate that we are only wheat growers? We are just as interested in all branches of agriculture as are the eastern provinces, your problems are our problems. I speak perhaps more as a grain grower than a stock raiser but I have some knowledge of the live stock industry and I am here to make any contribution I can towards the solution of its problems. These are our problems, and I think the proper place to discuss them is in the agriculture committee, with all sections of Canada represented. Do not divide the east against the west. I am sure the present Minister of Agriculture will agree with the ex-Minister of Agriculture and myself on that point. With the ex-Minister of Agriculture I say, again we have another illustration of the necessity for bringing all these branches of agriculture under one head. We in western Canada have always contended that the administration of the Canada Grain Act is not in the proper department of government. With all due respect to the officials of that department, we still believe that the administration of that act should be under the control of the Department of Agriculture.
I want to assure my hon. friend that in anything I say to-day I am merely endeavouring to accomplish the very thing he proposes to do when he advocates dividing the agriculture committee into two sections, but I say to him that he will never attain his object in the way he proposes. The proper method is for all the members interested in these problems which he has enumerated to bring up on the floor of the house any question that should be discussed with a view to solution, so that it might be referred by the government to the committee on agriculture, and as a westerner I can assure him that he will get one hundred per cent support from us in any effort that is made to solve the problems he has indicated.

As a member from western Canada, I have been studying this resolution and I have come to the conclusion that it is not advisable to have two sections, a wheat section and one on agri-' culture, in the agriculture committee. I would suggest that we divide the time. Last session the entire time was taken up talking about a wheat called garnet. Both the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), and the hon. gentleman who last spoke (Mr. Vallance), know very well that there were many serious problems connected with agriculture which it was important to bring before the house and which we had no opportunity of discussing. I will refer to a few of these matters now.
During the recess I passed through the west and I took occasion to look into the conditions of agriculture, and I tell you now that unless some drastic step is taken and taken at once to save agriculture from its present situation we shall never get anywhere in Canada. I do not think there should be any division such as is proposed. I want us to stretch our hands over that wide space, and say that we are all 'Canadians. We want to understand each other. There are several problems that I am going to mention and I should like the Minister of Agriculture to listen to me because I am going to talk about them in a practical way. Unless he does something with regard to these problems there is no hope for agriculture.
I want the minister to take note of the commercial marketing of live stock; let him go over the live stock yards east and west and find out what is taking place there. Call the men to one side and talk to them about the commercial marketing of live stock in the *stock yards at the various districts in the east and west, and you will see what is going on. I do not want it to be supposed that I am speaking for myself, for I am out of the business although I spent fifty-five years in the marketing of live stock products; but I am bound to say that there are many things .going on to-day that are positively injurious to the successful marketing of cattle in the various stock yards. The situation is appalling. You stand in the alley way and see one man in possession of the yard, the salesmen waiting for one buyer. They are right in the grip of the big interests. I make that statement because I know what I am talking about.
There is just one buyer in the yard and he can fix his own price. I say to the Minister of Agriculture that unless he puts ani end to the iniquitous system which is in operation now, of requiring a bond of S10,000 for a man to do business in the yards, he will kill every little man doing business in western Canada; he will put them all out of business. I say, give the little fellow a chance; give the man with $5,000 a chance to operate in the yard, and the big fellow will not get the innings he is having to-day. Why should you ask for a bond of $10,000? And I believe that in the city of Winnipeg it is $180,000. The man who would be the most active buyer in the yard is the little man who is working with $5,000 or $6,000, but he cannot do business when he has to put up $10,000. The present system was inaugurated by the late Minister of Agriculture and, it is said, was adopted to protect the shipper of live stock. Well, in the old days he did not ask for protection. He came with his live stock and sold them in the yard. Before he got his money he would lock the gate and he would say, "When I get my cheque I will give you delivery of these cattle." That is the way business was done at that time.
I want now to say a word or two in regard to the grading of hogs. Here again a most iniquitous system has been adopted in connection with the grading of these animals. I have here a letter from one of the best cattle men in the west, a live stock salesman, indicating this iniquitous system of the grading of hogs is playing into the hands of those who are buying hogs in the yard, to the detriment of the farmers. That system is worn out and should be abolished.

Why not shut out all products that come into competition with the products of our farms? farmers and the other districts of the province of Quebec, Everybody is aware that unless something is done immediately to hetlp the farming class, bankruptcy will appear everywhere. Many of our opponents are as well aware as I am of the farmers' plight and if one of these hon. members had the courage to rise in the house and request a bonus on butter, cheese or any other farm product, so as to help our farmers, he could rest assured that he would meet with no opposition on the part of the Liberal party.
I understand that the resolution under consideration requests that the committee on agriculture be divided into two sections, one of which would take up wheat and the other the dairy industry. If our western friends have obtained a bonus on wheat and if they obtain all they request., it is because they have the courage to rise in the house and set forth their claims. I have not the honour of being a member of the committee on agriculture and I do not know whether the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi is one. If there are no members opposite included in this committee, I trust that the eastern township members and those of Quebec who represent rural districts will be invited to appear before this committee in order to make known their grievances and the needs of the province of Quebec.
I make these few suggestions, hoping that they will be taken under consideration. I would request the hon. members who have had the honour to be elected in the Eastern Townships and in other rural constituencies of Quebec to do their utmost in order to improve the lot of the farming class and, this, as soon as possible. If nothing is done within the next few months, we shall certainly witness a complete bankruptcy of the farming community.

Representing a rural constituency
and being a member of the committee on agriculture and colonization, I deem it my duty, first, to extend my sincere congratulation to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) on the resolution which he introduced this afternoon, and then to express my humble views on the subject matter. When certain hon. members contend that this resolution purports to divide the we.st from the east, I wonder why they make such an assertion. In my opinion the resolution simply aims at granting more time to the study of the various agricultural problems.
I was present at most of the sittings of the committee on agriculture and I can assert, to my knowledge, that the question of wheat was always to the fore, except once when

eggs were discussed. I therefore think it wise to divide the committee on agriculture into two sections and have one group of members devote their time to farming in general. This will not be to the disadvantage of western farmers since they themselves state that they carry on mixed farming. We could study this subject, thus allowing more time to those who specialize in wheat growing.
Allow me to state, sir, that when one attends the committee on agriculture five or six times to discuss a subject which is of particular interest to him and finds that wheat takes up the whole time, this .subject in the long run appears tedious, especially if one hails from the outlying parts of the province of Quebec. If there existed a subdivision of this committee, we would likely appear more regularly at the sittings and take a greater interest in the discussion of problems which we have at heart.
It is unfortunate to note that hon. members of the opposition and especially those of Quebec, when it is a question of agriculture, are not broadminded enough in discussing this question outside of petty politics. Two of these hon. members this afternoon spoke on this resolution. Unfortunately, contentions were brought up, which I might characterize as false. The hon. member for St. Johnis-Iberville (Mr. Rheaume) states that agriculture is encouraged in the province of Quebec; let him request the Prime Minister of that province to settle the bill of $452 which is due to Mr. Wilfrid Ouellette, since January last.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with much
pleasure to the discussion which took place between my. friends from the province of Quebec, on both sides of the house. I congratulate the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) for having given us the opportunity of discussing the subject matter of this resolution, by moving that the agri-

Agriculture Committee-Mr. Mercier (St. Henri)
cultural question which interests both east and west be considered on an equal footing. I agree with him heartily.
Although being a city lawyer, I am somewhat acquainted and love the countryside. My forebears were farmers and it always gives me much pleasure to hear farming discussed, becauise Quebec, from the viewpoint of mixed farming, is the first province of confederation.
In this discussion I am particularly interested in the suggestions made to the Government by our friends on the right. They request an enquiry on milk. Very well! I am in favour of it. The farmers of Quebec are taken advantage of, there is no doubt about it. They are allowed seventy cents per hundred pounds of milk, as the honourable member for Rrome-Missisquoi stated, and, in many localities in Quebec, milk dealers allow farmers only what they themselves are willing to grant them. The milk producers are never certain of the price they will obtain for their product and they never know what amount is enclosed in the envelope which is forwarded by the butter or cheese factories. Milk is purchased very cheaply in the rural districts and it has been sold as high as eleven cents per quart in the cities; to-day, it is sold at ten cents a quart. As the honourable member for Brome-Missis-quoi, who made a special study of the question, stated, is it reasonable that milk distributors should make a profit of four to five dollars per hundred pounds? I state that it is a shameful exploitation and that no government should tolerate such a situation. Moreover, this milk is distributed to poverty stricken people and the Dominion Government pay one-third of the cost, the provincial government one-third, and the municipality the other third. This government is therefore interested in legislating on this question, in order to put an end to this exploitation and do justice to the consumers as well as the farmers.
If the farmer is too highly paid, we are charged too much; if the farmers are underpaid, we, city consumers, are still charged too much. A readjustment of prices must take place, this protection must not be granted to those who form part of trusts and exploit, first, the farmer and then the city consumer.
The same may be said of coal. An enquiry is at present being held on coal. I trust that it will not come out as dark as coal itself, that light will be thrown on the subject and the situation remedied. We are informed that coal is hardly worth seven dollars per ton delivered in Montreal, yet it is sold to consumers at fifteen and sixteen dollars per ton. There is no reason why coal should sell
at such high prices. There again the Dominion Government has an interest since it pays, in Montreal and in all cities of Quebec, one-third of the price of the coal which is supplied to those in need, the other two-thirds being paid by the province and the municipality. It is, therefore, in the government's interest to pay a lower price for this coal and they should refer the matter to the Labour Department in order that an inquiry may be held on trusts, as the members on the right have just requested on the milk trusts, for which I congratulate them.
It is all very well to ask that the Committee on Agriculture be divided into two sections, one on mixed farming and the other on wheat, but this committee embraces all the branches of agricultural activities in this country. If honourable members wish to be heard they have but to consult the rules of the House. If they have reason to complain, they have but to put their grievances in writing and muster up sufficient courage to bring them up in the House, even if they are not looked upon favourably by the government. We shall heed them and refer them to the Committee on Agriculture where they may be threshed out and justice done to farmers and consumers. Let them put in writing their complaints, let them place them on the order paper of the House and demand a vote. Notwithstanding all efforts brought to bear to have them withdrawn, under pretext that they might harm the government, let them see that they remain on the order paper of the House. Let them move their adoption, they will be put to a vote and if they have a majority they will be referred to the Committee on Agriculture where they will be given the time necessary so as to be discussed without any need of sub-dividing the committee into two sections. We shall help them, in the committee, to pass all the resolutions that they wish to introduce with a view to forcing the government to act, that is in case they should refuse to protect the farmers and prevent exploitation of consumers in the cities.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure it will give a good deal of satisfaction to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) that his resolution has provoked this discussion, showing the interest he has aroused. I shall be very brief.
In the 1931 session the agriculture committee held twenty-two meetings. Seventeen of these meetings were devoted to a reference from the agriculture committee, and all of the seventeen dealt with mixed farming, none with wheat. Among the items dealt with there was that of grading.
I think that if it were generally understood that our grading policies grew out of a demand from the producers themselves it would set at rest the minds of many people who perhaps do not thoroughly understand them and take exception to them. All that grading does is to put the highest quality product here, the second there, the third next and so on, so that the purchaser can have the benefit thereof in purchasing and it encourages our producers to turn out the highest quality.
Another problem discussed was that of milk prices. This is almost entirely a question for the provinces, and the provinces have taken very serious hold of it. At least two of the provinces have for the past few weeks or months, I believe, been engaged in
very serious and careful investigation of milk prices. The Quebec government, I believe, have almost finished their investigation. They have a few references to report upon yet, and the report is not printed but only in typewritten form. The Ontario government have also done a good deal of work in this connection.
With reference to the stock yard question, we have been in consultation with the various stock yard representatives throughout the dominion and they have before them now a request from the Department of Agriculture with regard to a reduction in the charges in stock yards. We hope to hear from them in the course of at least a week or two.
It is regrettable, in a house like this, representative of all Canada, that misrepresentation should unwittingly be made regarding a great body of farmers in the dominion. I can assure hon. members that if any of them think of going to western Canada they will still find a great number of farmers living there in the winter time and that they are not all in California.
After listening to the discussion, I cannot see any problem in connection with the division of the committee on agriculture. All hon. members from eastern Canada who have spoken have expressed themselves in favour of a fuller discussion of the problems of eastern Canadian agriculture, or agriculture apart from wheat; therefore they are agreed. And I believe that all western speakers have also spoken in favour of at least a perfectly full discussion of eastern problems in agriculture. Personally I think that there is ample room and opportunity within the committee on agriculture, as it is at present constituted, to discuss all these problems. The east will get the benefit of suggestions from the west, and the west will receive some suggestions from the older and more experienced agriculturists in the east. Therefore I should like to see this matter left as it is and brought up before the committee on agriculture, because no one listening to the discussion this afternoon can have any opinion but one, and that is the necessity for cooperation and for a full discussion of any agricultural problems that are placed before the committee.
